html:
The Urnfield culture was the main late Bronze Age culture of central Europe, from about 1300 to 750 BCE. It takes its name from its custom of burning the dead and burying their ashes in urns, in large cemeteries of flat graves.

It followed the Tumulus culture, whose people had buried their dead under mounds, and spread from the Danube lands across much of Europe, into Italy, France and as far west as the Pyrenees. Related groups to the north and east, such as the Lusatian culture, shared the rite.

Bronze working flourished. Urnfield smiths hammered sheet bronze into helmets, shields, armour and large vessels, and made new kinds of swords. Many hilltop settlements were fortified, which suggests more warfare. These were the same centuries as the Late Bronze Age collapse in the eastern Mediterranean.

The Urnfield culture led into the iron-using Hallstatt culture. It was once tied to the spread of the Celts; that link is now doubted, though some scholars still connect it with an early form of Celtic speech.
